description_full: Broadridge Financial Solutions, Inc. provides investor communications and technology-driven solutions for the financial services industry in the United States and internationally. The company's Investor Communication Solutions segment handles the proxy materials distribution and voting processes for bank, broker-dealer, corporate issuer, and fund clients; provides fund manager; and various other regulatory communication solutions. The segment also offers ProxyEdge, an institutional voting platform that allows institutional investors to view, manage, and vote multi-custodial holdings, as well as third party vote recommendations; data-driven analytics solutions; international corporate governance solutions; fiduciary-focused learning and development, software and technology, and data and analytics services, as well as automated mutual fund and exchange-traded funds trade processing; content management and omni-channel distribution platform; corporate solutions that revolve around shareholder meetings and proxy, corporate governance, regulatory filings and disclosure, and stock transfer services; corporate issuer solutions; and customer communications solutions. The Global Technology and Operations segment provides solutions that automate the front-to-back transaction lifecycle of equity, mutual fund, fixed income, foreign exchange and exchange-traded derivatives, order capture and execution, trade confirmation, margin, cash management, clearing and settlement, reference data management, reconciliations, securities financing and collateral management, asset servicing, compliance and regulatory reporting, portfolio accounting, and custody-related services. This segment also offers business process outsourcing services; technology solutions, such portfolio management, compliance, fee billing, and operational support solutions; and capital market and wealth and investment management solutions. The company was founded in 1962 and is headquartered in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Broadridge Financial Solutions, is a large-cap technology business with a $21.8B market cap on $7.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 8% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.20× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.6×.

Shareholder yield of 4.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Significant goodwill (42% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (38% annualized) adds uncertainty
Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
AI disruption of existing software moats — incumbents with durable margins face commoditisation as AI-native competitors replicate features at a fraction of the R&D cost.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 11% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Piotroski score 8/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
18 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Financial quality scores above most Technology peers

sect: Its 17% operating margin runs 11pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.74x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 24% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 12% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 17% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $161.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 27% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $171 (margin of safety -13%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $133 to $226 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 21.3 vs 27.4 and P/FCF 17.0 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 16% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $209 on average, 9% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 8.2%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.26).
It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.20x.
ROE of 40% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($403.8M of cash against $3.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 11.6x.
Goodwill makes up 42% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.2% over 3 years, 8.4% over 5 years and 9.9% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 32% of profits supports about 4.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 16.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 98%.
It returns 4.8% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 18 consecutive years, raising it 11.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 16,000 employees, each generates about $467K of revenue, 1.3x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 8.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $80K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (7x revenue per employee).
